holidays.name: National Ding-a-Ling Day
holidays.description: A day for embracing your silly side. You can call a friend, make a goofy phone joke, or just be a lovable ding-a-ling. It's a reminder not to take yourself too seriously during the busy holiday season.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It has become a favorite on quirky holiday calendars, and the name is usually linked to old-fashioned telephone ringing.
holidays.funFact: The word 'ding-a-ling' has been used as a playful word for a silly person for decades. It has also been used as an imitation of a bell or telephone ring.

holidays.name: Gingerbread House Day
holidays.description: A day for building, decorating and nibbling on little candy-covered cottages made of gingerbread. Frosting glue, gumdrop roof tiles and peppermint pathways are all encouraged. A leaning wall is welcome too.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It falls in the middle of the holiday baking season, when gingerbread houses are most popular.
holidays.funFact: Gingerbread houses are often linked to German holiday baking traditions. Many people trace their popularity to the fairy tale of Hansel and Gretel, in which the children find a house made of sweets.

holidays.name: National Poinsettia Day
holidays.description: A day to appreciate the bright red, star-shaped plant that decorates homes and offices every December. It's also a chance to learn that the colorful 'petals' are not flowers at all.
holidays.origin: The observance honors Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first U.S. Minister to Mexico, who introduced the plant to the United States. He died on December 12, 1851, and the day was set aside to mark that anniversary.
holidays.funFact: The poinsettia's colorful parts are modified leaves called bracts. The actual flowers are the tiny yellow clusters in the center.
